alternative: Ractor workers (parallel, but experimental and message-only) or a process pool (Process.fork with pipes, or the Parallel gem) for CPU-bound work; Thread + Queue pools only for I/O-bound joins.
idiom_name: none; Ractor workers or process pools are the substitute
implementation_notes: CRuby runs Ruby code under a Global VM Lock, so Threads give concurrency but not CPU parallelism - a recursive thread fork/join is faster to write, not faster to run. Ractors are the language's parallel unit (the GVL is held per ractor, and the docs note that ractors can perform in parallel without locking each other), but they are explicitly experimental, forbid sharing ordinary objects and ship no work-stealing scheduler: you fork ractors and join manually with take/yield or messages. For CPU-bound fork/join the practical answers are worker processes (Process.fork with pipes, or the Parallel gem) or Ractor workers; keep Thread + Queue for joins that merely wait on I/O, where the GVL is released.
code_sketch:
# CPU-bound: one GVL blocks thread parallelism; Ractors run in parallel
workers = slices.map { |s| Ractor.new(s) { |part| heavy(part) } }  # fork
values  = workers.map(&:take)                                        # join
total   = values.sum
# Ractor.new prints an experimental warning; objects cross by copy or move.
pitfalls: Ractor blocks are isolated: they cannot read outer variables (ArgumentError), and objects cross by deep copy or move: true - copying large slices is expensive.
Thread + Queue joins only overlap I/O: CPU-bound leaves serialize under the GVL no matter how many threads are spawned.
Forked child processes do not return values implicitly - a pipe/socket protocol must carry partial results back, and each child must be waited on or zombies accumulate.
